addressed_problems.content: Early-Time (ET) tickets reduce the computational cost of searching for winning tickets in deep Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) by using a smaller number of timesteps during the search process, but the resulting subnetworks do not exactly match the performance of winning tickets obtained with the full timestep Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP). This introduces an accuracy–computational‑cost tradeoff that is especially noticeable at extreme sparsity levels (e.g., ≥95%). Quantifying this tradeoff across different SNN architectures (e.g., VGG16, ResNet19) and datasets (e.g., CIFAR10, CIFAR100), and developing principled methods to control the gap while maximizing search speed, remains an open problem.

The performance of the Early‑Time (ET) ticket and Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) in deep SNNs is sensitive to key hyperparameters: the KL divergence threshold λ for selecting the early timestep and the rewinding epoch for IMP. The paper reports empirical defaults (λ=0.6, rewind epoch=20) that work across several datasets, but these choices are not systematically optimized nor theoretically justified. In high‑sparsity regimes (≥95%), incorrect selection of the rewinding epoch can cause accuracy drops of ~1.5%, and the optimal λ may vary with architecture or dataset. Developing a principled framework for setting these hyperparameters—or making the methods robust to their choice—remains an unresolved issue.

Transferring winning tickets discovered in Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) to Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) offers a way to bypass the expensive search cost of IMP on SNNs. This approach works well for simple datasets (SVHN, Fashion‑MNIST), maintaining less than 2% accuracy drop even at 98.13% sparsity. However, on more complex datasets (CIFAR10, CIFAR100), the transferred tickets fail at high sparsity levels (≥95%), showing a large performance drop. Understanding why the structural differences between ANN and SNN (e.g., ReLU vs. Leaky‑Integrate‑and‑Fire neuron, surrogate gradient approximation) cause this breakdown, and whether adapted transfer schemes (e.g., fine‑tuning the mask or initialization) can close the gap, is an open scientific question.

Pruning‑at‑initialization methods, such as SNIP, that rely on gradient magnitudes to score weight importance fail in Spiking Neural Networks because the backward gradients are approximated through a non‑differentiable surrogate function of the Leaky‑Integrate‑and‑Fire (LIF) neuron. Experiments show that SNIP on SNNs yields accuracy worse than random pruning at sparsities above 80%, in contrast to its effectiveness in ANNs. Designing initialization‑time scoring metrics that account for the temporal dynamics and non‑differentiability of spiking neurons—so that sparse subnetworks can be identified before any training—remains an open challenge for efficient SNN compression.

While Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) pruning achieves high weight sparsity (up to 97%) in deep SNNs, it does not reduce the number of spikes per inference, as spike counts remain similar across sparsity levels. Since the energy consumption of SNNs on neuromorphic hardware depends on both memory access (affected by weight sparsity) and spike‑driven MAC operations (affected by spike rate), achieving joint reductions requires co‑design of pruning with temporal or spike‑rate mechanisms. Developing pruning strategies that simultaneously minimize memory movement and spike energy—e.g., by encouraging spike sparsity alongside weight sparsity—is an open engineering and scientific problem.

Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) are a biologically inspired class of low‑power neural models that process inputs as discrete spikes over multiple timesteps using Leak‑Integrate‑and‑Fire (LIF) neurons. Prior to this work, SNN research had advanced training methods (surrogate gradients) and deeper architectures (e.g., VGG16 and ResNet19 variants for SNNs), but practical deployment on memory‑ and compute‑constrained neuromorphic/edge hardware remained limited by model size and search cost for sparse networks. Existing SNN pruning methods largely targeted shallow SNNs (2–7 layers) and relied on layer‑specific heuristics, thresholding, or optimization schemes (e.g., ADMM or soft‑pruning) that were not demonstrated at the scale of modern deep SNN architectures. At the same time, Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) and Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) in ANNs had shown that dense networks contain sparse subnetworks ("winning tickets") that match dense performance, but applying LTH to SNNs poses two interrelated gaps: (1) it was unknown whether winning tickets exist in deep SNNs whose neuronal dynamics (multi‑timestep LIF integrate/fire and surrogate gradients) differ substantially from ReLU ANNs, and (2) the canonical search procedure for winning tickets (IMP or similar iterative schemes) is computationally heavy for SNNs because each training pass involves multiple timesteps per sample, making iterative initialization–training–pruning–retraining prohibitively expensive at large depth and high sparsity. These gaps prevented reliable, scalable construction of highly sparse deep SNNs (e.g., ≥90% sparsity) with controlled accuracy loss and practical search time on GPU/edge hardware.

nodes.content: In deep visual‑recognition SNNs (VGG16/ResNet19 architectures trained with surrogate gradients and T timesteps), practitioners needed sparsification methods that could reduce parameter memory while preserving accuracy for deployment on memory‑limited neuromorphic/edge devices. Prior SNN pruning literature demonstrated substantial sparsity only on shallow SNNs (2–7 conv layers) using thresholding, online heuristics, or optimization‑based compression; those methods had not been validated on much deeper SNNs that employ multistep LIF dynamics and batch normalization. Without evidence that LTH‑style winning tickets exist in deep SNNs, there was no principled way to obtain extremely sparse (≫90%) deep SNNs with predictable accuracy behavior; consequently, designers could not rely on LTH approaches to produce compact deep SNNs for realistic image benchmarks (CIFAR10/100) or compare against dense baselines in a reproducible manner.

To validate LTH in SNNs one must run the IMP cycle of train→prune→reinitialize→retrain many times. In SNNs each training epoch incurs multiple forward/backward passes across T timesteps per sample (e.g., default T=5), multiplying per‑epoch cost relative to ANNs. Existing reports of IMP efficiency were centered on ANNs; there was no quantified understanding of the wall‑clock cost to obtain extreme sparsity winning tickets in deep SNNs, so it was unclear whether IMP was practically usable for deep SNN model compression on available GPU resources. This computational bottleneck prevented widespread adoption of IMP for deep SNN pruning and blocked exploration of very high sparsity regimes.

IMP yields high‑quality sparse SNNs but its iterative nature imposes heavy compute costs. EB was proposed in ANNs to detect stable masks early and cut search time, but EB had not been evaluated for deep SNNs with multistep dynamics. Without an SNN‑validated EB analysis, there was no demonstrated lower‑cost alternative to IMP for SNNs that could enable practical winning‑ticket discovery. Additionally, it was unknown whether EB's early mask detection would generalize across SNN training dynamics and whether EB would be able to produce winning tickets at very high sparsity for complex vision datasets; this gap left open whether EB could be a practical replacement for IMP at scale.

The multi‑timestep nature of SNN training provides an unexplored axis for efficiency: if the subnetworks important for T timesteps can be identified from training at fewer timesteps, the per‑epoch cost during mask search could be proportionally reduced. Prior pruning heuristics operated purely in the spatial/weight dimension and did not exploit temporal redundancy of early timesteps. Without a principled selection method for a reduced timestep (T_early) that preserves mask quality, any timestep‑reduction approach risked producing masks that fail after retraining with full T. The KL divergence between accumulated outputs provides a statistical measure of representational similarity across timesteps, enabling selection of a minimal T_early; prior to this work there was no validated ET procedure combining a timestep selection criterion with standard winning‑ticket search methods for deep SNNs.

Searching winning tickets in SNNs is more expensive than ANNs due to multistep dynamics; prior LTH work in ANNs suggested transferring masks across tasks or architectures to save search cost. It was unknown whether winning tickets obtained from ANN training (cheaper to run) could be reused directly by SNNs (which have different activation dynamics and surrogate gradients). If full transfer were possible, one could avoid expensive SNN IMP searches by searching in ANN space; without empirical transferability characterization across dataset complexities and sparsity regimes, practitioners lacked guidance on when ANN→SNN transfer would be effective or when SNN‑native searching was still required.

Methods that identify important connections at initialization (e.g., SNIP) aim to eliminate any training‑time search. These methods rely on reliable gradient information at t=0 to score connections. However, SNNs use non‑differentiable LIF neurons and surrogate gradient approximations during training; the compatibility of initialization‑based sensitivity measures with surrogate gradients in SNNs was unknown. If initialization scores are unreliable in SNNs, pruning at initialization would not be a viable low‑cost strategy for deep SNN sparsification, leaving practitioners reliant on training‑time search methods.

A practical question in structured or unstructured pruning is whether to prune each layer equally (local pruning) or to prune globally across the network. Prior SNN pruning work had not systematically compared these strategies at the scale of deep SNNs. Using equal per‑layer pruning percentages can overly damage certain layers and reduce final accuracy at high sparsity; without an empirical recommendation for deep SNNs, practitioners could choose suboptimal pruning regimes that inhibit reaching extreme sparsity with acceptable accuracy.

One target of SNN compression is reducing run‑time energy via fewer spikes and sparser weights. It was conceivable that pruning could also reduce event activity (spike counts), further lowering energy, but prior to systematic measurement it was unclear whether LTH‑derived weight sparsity would lead to lower spike rates. Without this information, designers could not quantify the net energy benefit of weight sparsity alone on neuromorphic hardware, nor determine whether additional mechanisms were necessary to reduce spike rates for MAC energy savings.

The standard IMP recipe rewinds to initialization; Frankle et al. proposed Late Rewinding to stabilize mask discovery in ANNs. For deep SNNs with surrogate gradients and multistep dynamics, the impact of rewind epoch on final sparse accuracy was unknown. If rewinding to the wrong epoch degrades performance at high sparsity, practitioners need guidance on rewinding to obtain robust winning tickets; lacking that, IMP outcomes for deep SNNs could be unstable across random seeds and epochs, compromising reproducibility and applicability.

A dense deep spiking neural network (SNN) trained with surrogate-gradient backpropagation contains sparse subnetworks ("winning tickets") that achieve comparable test accuracy to the unpruned dense SNN: using Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) with Late Rewinding (rewinding to epoch 20) and a pruning ratio of 25% per iteration over 15 pruning iterations, experiments on VGG16 and ResNet19 SNNs across datasets SVHN, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR10 and CIFAR100 demonstrate winning tickets at up to approximately 97.5% sparsity with small accuracy degradation (for example, on ResNet19/CIFAR10 the baseline accuracy 93.22% is preserved within −0.04% at 97.54% sparsity). A winning ticket is defined as the subnetwork f(x; θ ⊙ m) obtained by pruning the 25% lowest-magnitude weights per IMP iteration from the dense network f(x; θ) and reinitializing the remaining weights to their values at epoch 20 (Late Rewinding).

metadata.narrative: The existence claim is strongly supported by H1, which shows IMP outperforms prior methods on the tested architecture, and H2, which confirms replicability across seeds. However, P1 and P3 limit the scope of the conclusion: the evidence is drawn from only two architectures and fixed hyperparameters, making it uncertain whether the claim extends to the full class of deep SNNs. P2 additionally shows that the phrase "small accuracy degradation" is inconsistently applied across datasets, with CIFAR100 experiencing a ~2.3% drop at 97% sparsity, which undermines the quantitative claim for complex datasets. The interaction is that H1 and H2 robustly establish winning tickets for VGG16/ResNet19 on simple-to-moderate datasets, but the residual risks from P1, P3, and P2 mean the overall conclusion should be scoped to those architectures and hyperparameters, with degraded performance acknowledged for CIFAR100 at extreme sparsity.

nodes.title: Winning tickets exist in deep SNNs up to ~97.5% sparsity with small accuracy degradation

nodes.content: Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP), applied with Late Rewinding (rewinding to epoch 20) and a pruning ratio of 25% per iteration, discovers high-quality winning tickets in deep SNNs (achieving top accuracies across sparsity levels), but the iterative search is computationally costly for SNNs: measured GPU search times on an RTX 2080Ti GPU with batch size 128 and timestep T=5 range from tens to approximately 70 hours for extreme sparsity (e.g., IMP search time for ResNet19 on CIFAR10 reaches 73.54 hours for 98.13% target sparsity), and searching for ≥95% sparsity requires on the order of dozens of GPU hours per configuration.

metadata.narrative: H3 provides a substantial empirical characterization of IMP search time across sparsity levels, architectures, and datasets, which strongly supports the claim that IMP is computationally expensive. P4 notes that absolute hour figures are hardware-dependent, but the qualitative conclusion of high cost is robust to this. P5 notes the absence of comparison to other search methods, but this does not significantly weaken the claim since the high absolute hours already demonstrate expensiveness. The interaction is that H3 carries the credit, and P4/P5 are minor refinements that do not threaten the core conclusion; thus the conclusion holds with high credibility.

nodes.title: IMP finds high-quality winning tickets but requires up to 73.54 GPU hours for 98.13% sparsity

nodes.content: Early-Bird (EB) ticket detection (monitoring mask stability across a time window of q=5 epochs with a threshold τ=0.02, using unstructured weight pruning) discovers stable pruning masks early in training and dramatically reduces winning-ticket search time (search often completes within ≲2 hours on an RTX 2080Ti GPU). However, EB fails to discover winning tickets at very high sparsity on complex image datasets: EB reliably finds winning tickets at sparsities up to approximately 95% for simple datasets (SVHN, Fashion-MNIST) but cannot reach winning tickets at sparsities above 95% on CIFAR10 and CIFAR100 (accuracy degrades substantially above that sparsity).

metadata.narrative: H4 and H5 together establish that EB significantly reduces search time and provide a clear empirical boundary (works on simple datasets up to >95% sparsity, fails on CIFAR10/100 beyond ~95%). P6 and P7 qualify this boundary: the failure may be specific to the chosen hyperparameters (q, τ, unstructured pruning) and may not generalize to all SNN architectures. The interaction is that H4 and H5 give high confidence in the search-time improvement and the observed failure, but P6 raises the possibility that tuning could extend EB's reach, and P7 questions generalization. The overall conclusion that EB cannot reach highest sparsities on complex datasets is supported for the tested configurations, but the possibility of extending EB via hyperparameter tuning or to other architectures is not ruled out.

nodes.title: EB tickets reduce search time to <2 hours but fail above 95% sparsity on complex datasets

nodes.content: Early-Time (ET) ticket is a temporal search-cost reduction technique for spiking neural networks (SNNs) that finds the important weight connectivity for an SNN trained for T timesteps by first training with a smaller timestep T_early < T selected via a Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence similarity criterion. Let P_t denote the class probability vector obtained by accumulating output activations from timestep 1 to t. ET uses the KL divergence D_KL(P_t || P_T) = Σ_x P_t(x) ln(P_t(x)/P_T(x)), normalized by D_KL(P_2 || P_T); the smallest t in {2,...,T-1} with normalized D_KL < λ (with λ=0.6) is chosen as T_early. ET is applied to the winning-ticket search procedure F(·) (either IMP or EB): first discover the mask using F with T_early, then train the pruned network at the original T. Empirically, ET combined with IMP or EB reduces winning-ticket search time substantially (measured speedups up to ×1.66 on RTX 2080Ti) while incurring small accuracy reductions (≤1% drop for sparsity <95% in many experiments). ET can be determined stably after a small number of initial epochs (N=2 used for stability in experiments).

metadata.narrative: H6, H7, and H8 collectively provide strong evidence for the ET approach: the core premise (connections from fewer timesteps are reusable) is validated in preliminary experiments, the KL selection is stable, and the method consistently reduces search time with acceptable accuracy drops in full evaluations. P8 and P9 identify residual uncertainties: the threshold λ=0.6 is untuned and may not be optimal, and the preliminary experiment used one-shot pruning rather than iterative mask search. However, H8 directly addresses the iterative search scenario (IMP+ET, EB+ET) and shows the method works, mitigating P9's concern. P8 remains a valid point: the choice of λ could affect results, and the paper does not provide a systematic analysis of this trade-off. The overall conclusion holds with good confidence for the tested λ=0.6, but the general recommendation of λ=0.6 across all settings is weakly justified.

nodes.title: ET ticket selects a smaller timestep via normalized KL divergence to reduce search time by up to ×1.59

nodes.content: Winning tickets (mask + initialization) discovered by IMP on artificial neural networks (ANNs) using ReLU activation can transfer to spiking neural networks (SNNs) by replacing ReLU with Leaky-Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) neurons and training in the SNN framework, with modest success at low to moderate sparsity: for simple datasets (SVHN, Fashion-MNIST) the transferred tickets show less than 2% accuracy drop even at extreme sparsity in some reported runs, but on more complex datasets (CIFAR10, CIFAR100) transferred tickets exhibit large accuracy degradation at high sparsity (≥95%), demonstrating that ANN and SNN winning tickets share only partial commonality and that ANN-based searching cannot fully substitute SNN search for high-sparsity targets.

metadata.narrative: H9 and H10 provide a broad empirical map of transferability, establishing that transfer fails on complex datasets at high sparsity while succeeding on simple datasets. P10 raises a potential confounding factor: the ANN training details are unspecified, leaving open the possibility that better-trained ANN tickets could transfer better on complex datasets. P11 notes the limited architecture scope. H9 partially mitigates P11 by covering two architectures and four datasets, but the failure pattern could still be architecture-dependent. The interaction is that H9/H10 strongly support the conclusion within the testbed, but P10 introduces a non-trivial risk that the observed failure is partly due to suboptimal ANN training rather than fundamental incompatibility. The conclusion remains credible but with moderate residual uncertainty.

nodes.title: ANN→SNN transferred winning tickets show limited transferability at high sparsity on complex datasets

nodes.content: The pruning-at-initialization method SNIP (single-shot pruning via connection sensitivity computed from initial backward gradients) fails to produce working winning tickets for deep SNNs: SNIP produces large performance degradation at high sparsity (>80%) on VGG16/CIFAR10 and can perform worse than random pruning in the reported experiments. The authors attribute this failure to the non-differentiable spiking neuron dynamics and the surrogate/approximated backward gradients used for training SNNs, which undermine SNIP's gradient-based importance estimates at initialization.

metadata.narrative: H11 provides strong comparative evidence that SNIP fails more severely in SNNs than in ANNs on VGG16/CIFAR10. P12 limits the generalization: only one architecture is tested, so the conclusion that SNIP is ineffective for all SNNs is under-supported. P13 notes that the attribution to non-differentiability is not experimentally validated by varying surrogate functions. The interaction is that H11 establishes the empirical phenomenon for one configuration, but P12 and P13 mean the conclusion should be scoped to similar architectures and the causal explanation is speculative. The conclusion holds as an empirical observation for VGG16, but broad claims about SNIP incompatibility with SNNs require further evidence.

nodes.title: SNIP fails to produce winning tickets in deep SNNs, performing worse than random pruning above 80% sparsity

nodes.content: Global magnitude pruning (prune across all weights to meet a global sparsity target) yields better accuracy in deep SNNs than applying the same per-layer local pruning percentages; under global pruning on VGG16/CIFAR10, layer-wise sparsity profiles show that deeper layers end up with higher sparsity than shallow layers at the overall target sparsity, and global pruning achieves superior performance especially at high target sparsities.

metadata.narrative: H12 provides a clear quantitative demonstration of global pruning's superiority and deeper-layer sparsity for VGG16/CIFAR10. P14 limits the scope: only one architecture is tested, and the conclusion may not hold for residual networks. The interaction is that H12 fully supports the claim for VGG16, but the generalization to deep SNNs broadly (including ResNet) is uncertain. The conclusion is well-supported for VGG16-type sequential architectures but should be considered tentative for ResNet.

nodes.title: Global pruning outperforms local pruning in SNNs; deeper layers achieve higher sparsity under global pruning

nodes.content: Across experiments pruning with Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP), the number of spikes per image (the operational event count that largely determines SNN MAC energy) remains approximately constant over a wide range of weight sparsities: sparse SNNs obtained via lottery ticket hypothesis (LTH) maintain similar spike rates compared to dense networks in the reported CIFAR10 experiments for VGG16 and ResNet19, implying that weight sparsity from LTH primarily reduces memory footprint and memory-movement energy rather than lowering spike-driven compute energy.

metadata.narrative: H13 provides strong empirical evidence that total spike count does not decrease with LTH weight sparsity on CIFAR10 for two architectures. P15 raises generalization concerns: the result may not hold for event-based datasets or other pruning methods. P16 notes that per-layer spikes could vary, but the conclusion about total energy (which integrates layer counts) remains correct, so P16 is a minor refinement. The interaction is that H13 robustly establishes the claim for the tested settings, while P15 indicates the claim's scope is limited to static image datasets and IMP-derived sparsity. The conclusion holds with good credibility for its demonstrated scope.

nodes.title: Weight sparsity from LTH does not reduce spike counts; spike energy remains similar across sparsity levels

nodes.content: Using Late Rewinding (rewind to weights at epoch i instead of initial random weights) improves IMP stability for deep SNNs: rewinding to intermediate epochs (the authors used epoch 20) produces better performance at high sparsity than rewinding to initialization, but the choice of rewinding epoch affects accuracy in extreme sparsity regimes (e.g., at 98.13% sparsity accuracy can drop nontrivially, such as ~1.5% drop when rewinding epoch is 260 on VGG16/CIFAR10), indicating that careful rewind-epoch selection is required when applying IMP to deep SNNs.

metadata.narrative: H14 provides a clear demonstration that rewinding epoch affects final accuracy at extreme sparsity for VGG16/CIFAR10. P17 notes that this evidence is from a single configuration, so the claim that "rewinding epoch selection affects extreme‑sparsity results" is supported for that configuration but may not generalize to other architectures/datasets. The interaction is that H14 fully supports the qualitative claim for the tested case, but the quantitative details (shape of the curve) may differ elsewhere. The conclusion that careful selection is required is well-supported for VGG16/CIFAR10, but the generality is uncertain.

nodes.title: Late Rewinding stabilizes IMP for deep SNNs; rewinding epoch selection affects accuracy at extreme sparsity

nodes.content: Winning tickets achieving comparable dense accuracy exist at sparsities up to 97% in deep SNNs specifically for VGG16 and ResNet19 architectures using Leaky-Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) neurons with surrogate-gradient backpropagation, trained on SVHN, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR10, and CIFAR100 datasets with timestep T=5, using Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) with Late Rewinding to epoch 20 and a pruning ratio of 25% per iteration. The existence of winning tickets in deep SNNs has not been established for other architectures (e.g., those with different neuron models, temporal coding schemes, adaptive thresholds, or deeper than 19 layers) or for different training protocols (e.g., direct-input encoding vs. rate coding, alternative surrogate gradient functions).

metadata.failure_mode: If the experimental evidence does not generalize to other deep SNN architectures or training protocols, then the conclusion as stated ("winning tickets exist in deep SNNs") would be falsely overbroad. The conclusion would still be valid for VGG16 and ResNet19 with the specific surrogate gradient and datasets, but its practical applicability to the broader class of deep SNNs (e.g., those using different neuron dynamics or temporal encodings) would be unsupported, narrowing the claim's utility for guiding general SNN compression deployment.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper tests only two specific deep architectures (VGG16 and ResNet19) and four datasets; the architectures cover a narrow region of design space (standard CNN-based classification with LIF neurons, surrogate gradients). There is no evidence from architectures with different neuron models (e.g., Izhikevich, adaptive LIF) or from SNNs that employ temporal coding (e.g., first-spike time) rather than rate coding. The surrogate gradient used (SpikingJelly default) may not be representative. The field of SNN architecture design is rapidly expanding, and it is plausible that winning tickets may not exist in certain regimes (e.g., very deep accuracies with high temporal resolution). Thus, the claim’s scope is uncertain.

nodes.title: Experimental evidence supports existence of winning tickets only in two architectures and four datasets for deep SNNs

nodes.content: For a deep SNN (ResNet19) trained on CIFAR100 with IMP and Late Rewinding (epoch 20), the accuracy drop at 97.54% sparsity is 2.29% relative to the dense baseline of 71.34% (resulting accuracy 69.05%). In contrast, for the same architecture on CIFAR10, the accuracy drop at similar sparsity is only 0.04% (baseline 93.22%, resulting accuracy 93.18%). The variation in accuracy drop across datasets makes the term "small accuracy degradation" ambiguous.

metadata.failure_mode: If the accuracy drop at 97% sparsity on complex datasets is not considered "small" by practitioners, then the conclusion that winning tickets achieve "small accuracy degradation" up to 97% sparsity is only valid for datasets similar to CIFAR10/SVHN/F-MNIST, not for CIFAR100. This would mean the claim is overextended to CIFAR100, potentially misleading designers who expect small degradation on that dataset at extreme sparsity.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper does not define a quantitative threshold for "small accuracy degradation." The baseline accuracy for CIFAR100 is 71.34%, and the 2.29% absolute drop at 97.54% sparsity is a relative drop of 3.2%; in many practical applications, such a degradation may not be considered small. The paper's Table 2 reports the drops explicitly, so the factual basis is present, but the conclusion language ("small accuracy degradation") overstates the consistency across datasets. The claimed scope "up to ~97% sparsity" for CIFAR100 is associated with a degradation that is arguably not small, making the conclusion's phrasing misleading for high-complexity datasets.

nodes.title: Accuracy degradation magnitude at 97.54% sparsity differs between CIFAR10 and CIFAR100

nodes.content: The IMP procedure used to establish the existence of winning tickets in deep SNNs employs fixed hyperparameters: pruning ratio p=25% per iteration, total iterations K=15, and Late Rewinding to epoch 20. The sensitivity of the existence claim to these choices across all datasets and architectures has not been tested; only the rewinding epoch was partially tested on VGG16/CIFAR10, where accuracy is stable up to 95.69% sparsity but shows a ~1.5% drop at 98.13% sparsity when rewinding epoch is set to 260. It is uncertain whether alternative settings (e.g., different p or K) would preserve the existence of winning tickets at the same sparsity levels, or whether the specific choices (p=25%, K=15, rewinding epoch=20) are critical for achieving >95% sparsity.

metadata.failure_mode: If different hyperparameters (e.g., p=20% or K=20) do not yield winning tickets at similar sparsity levels, then the conclusion that winning tickets exist in deep SNNs would be tied to a particular experimental protocol, making it less robust. The claim would be valid only under that protocol, which reduces its generality and practical confidence.
metadata.weakness_reason: The choice of pruning ratio and total iterations can affect which subnetworks are found and whether they achieve comparable accuracy. In ANNs, IMP has been shown to be sensitive to these choices. The paper does not provide a sensitivity analysis for p or K, nor does it justify why 25% and 15 were chosen. The rewinding epoch is analyzed for one architecture/dataset but not for others. Thus, the robustness of the existence result to these methodological choices is unknown, and the claim may be contingent on these specific values.

nodes.title: Winning-ticket existence at >95% sparsity may depend on specific IMP hyperparameter choices

nodes.content: The winning-ticket search time for Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) on a deep SNN, such as ResNet19 on CIFAR10 with batch size 128 and timestep T=5, measured on an RTX 2080Ti GPU, is 73.54 hours at 98.13% sparsity. This search time depends on the specific GPU hardware, software stack, and implementation efficiency; therefore, the numerical values are not directly transferable to other platforms such as edge devices or cloud GPUs, although the relative cost pattern (IMP is computationally expensive) is robust.

metadata.failure_mode: If on faster hardware the absolute time is much lower (e.g., 10 hours instead of 73), the conclusion that "IMP requires over 50 hours on GPU" would be false for that hardware, potentially misleading practitioners about the practical feasibility. The qualitative "expensive" conclusion remains, but the specific quantitative framing in the abstract (e.g., "IMP requires over 50 hours") is overgeneralized.
metadata.weakness_reason: The search times are measured on a single GPU model (RTX 2080Ti) under one implementation (PyTorch, SpikingJelly). Hardware capabilities vary widely, and optimizations (e.g., mixed-precision training, custom kernels) could significantly alter wall-clock times. The paper does not measure timing on other hardware or report flops or relative cost (e.g., ratio to ANN IMP time), which would make the claim more robust. Thus, the absolute hours should be interpreted with caution.

nodes.title: IMP search time of 73.54 hours for ResNet19/CIFAR10 is specific to RTX 2080Ti hardware

nodes.content: The cost of IMP for deep SNNs has not been compared with alternative search methods such as evolutionary search or Bayesian optimization, nor with the cost of training a dense SNN to convergence. Without such comparisons, the designation of IMP as computationally expensive lacks a baseline relative to other viable methods for achieving high sparsity in SNNs.

metadata.failure_mode: If there exist other methods with similar or higher cost that are commonly used, the claim that IMP is expensive could be misinterpreted as uniquely expensive. The conclusion that IMP is computationally expensive is still correct but its practical significance is ambiguous without benchmarks.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper uses EB as a lower-cost alternative, but does not compare IMP's cost to methods like non-iterative pruning (e.g., one-shot magnitude pruning with retraining) or to the cost of simply training a smaller dense network from scratch. The phrase "computationally expensive" is context-dependent; without anchor comparisons, the strength of the claim is vague. However, given that SNN training itself is costly, the large hours (50-70h) do support expensiveness.

nodes.title: IMP computational expense is assessed without comparison to alternative search methods for high-sparsity SNNs

nodes.content: The Early-Bird (EB) ticket detection in SNNs uses unstructured weight pruning with hyperparameters q=5 (time window) and τ=0.02 (mask stability threshold). The hyperparameters q=5 and τ=0.02 are used for EB ticket detection with unstructured weight pruning. Alternative q and τ values, as well as structured pruning as in the original EB work, have not been explored. It is possible that different EB configurations could succeed at sparsities exceeding 95% on CIFAR10 and CIFAR100.

metadata.failure_mode: If an alternative EB configuration (e.g., q=3, τ=0.05, or using channel pruning) yields winning tickets at >95% sparsity on CIFAR10/100, then the conclusion that EB "cannot reach highest sparsities on complex datasets" would be false under those configurations. The conclusion would need to be scoped to the specific hyperparameters used, reducing its generality.
metadata.weakness_reason: The EB ticket paper (You et al.) originally used channel pruning; the authors adopt unstructured weight pruning to match sparsity levels with IMP. The hyperparameters q and τ are fixed to values from the original paper (likely optimized for ANNs with channel pruning) without re-tuning for SNNs or for unstructured pruning. The mask detection algorithm's behavior may differ with pruning type and network dynamics. Without a sensitivity analysis, the reported failure at high sparsity may be an artifact of suboptimal EB configuration rather than a fundamental limitation of EB for SNNs.

nodes.title: EB ticket failure at >95% sparsity may depend on hyperparameter choices and pruning type

nodes.content: EB ticket detection fails to produce winning tickets at sparsity exceeding 95% on CIFAR10 and CIFAR100 for both VGG16 and ResNet19. The failure of EB at >95% sparsity has been tested only on VGG16 and ResNet19 on CIFAR10/100. It has not been tested on other deep SNN architectures such as ResNet34 or datasets with different complexity such as TinyImageNet.

metadata.failure_mode: If EB does work at high sparsity on other deep SNN architectures (e.g., ResNet34-TinyImageNet or a VGG variant with different BN), then the conclusion that EB "cannot reach highest sparsities on complex datasets" would be false for those architectures. The claim would need to be scoped to VGG16/ResNet19 on CIFAR10/100, which narrows its intended generality as stated in the conclusion title.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper's empirical basis for EB failure is limited to two architectures and two datasets. The original EB paper reported success across various architectures/datasets in ANNs. Given SNN dynamics differ, it's plausible that EB could work on other architectures (e.g., with different BN placement or residual connections) even at high sparsity. The conclusion's generality is unsupported.

nodes.title: EB failure at >95% sparsity only verified on VGG16 and ResNet19 on CIFAR10/100

nodes.content: The Early-Time (ET) ticket method selects T_early as the smallest timestep t in {2,3,4} such that the normalized KL divergence D_KL(P_t||P_T)/D_KL(P_2||P_T) < λ, with λ=0.6. The accuracy-computational cost trade-off for different λ values across architectures and datasets is not shown. A poorly chosen λ could select too small a T_early, risking accuracy loss, or too large a T_early, reducing speedup. The observed reduction in search time with ≤1% accuracy drop at sparsity below 95% depends on the specific choice λ=0.6.

metadata.failure_mode: If a different λ value (e.g., 0.5 or 0.7) leads to a significantly larger accuracy drop or smaller speedup for some configurations, the reported "≤1% drop" and speedup factors may not be representative. Practitioners using the ET method without re-tuning λ could see suboptimal results, undermining the practical recommendation.
metadata.weakness_reason: The KL divergence threshold λ directly determines T_early. The paper only shows the relationship between λ and T_early (Fig. 7(b)) but does not report accuracy results for different λ values. The choice λ=0.6 is adopted across all experiments without justification. There is no guarantee that this threshold minimizes accuracy loss or provides optimal speedup; it may accidentally favor one dataset over another. In machine learning, hyperparameters that govern important algorithmic choices should be validated.

nodes.title: ET ticket search-time reduction and accuracy drop depend on unoptimized KL divergence threshold λ=0.6

nodes.content: The preliminary experiment supporting the feasibility of ET uses a one-shot post-training magnitude pruning scheme: train a dense SNN with timestep T_pre, prune p% of low-magnitude weights, reinitialize, retrain with timestep T_post=5. The ET ticket method uses iterative mask search (IMP or EB) with the reduced timestep T_early during the search process itself. The preliminary experiment does not include iterative pruning, mask reinitialization, or the effect of Late Rewinding. The transferability of the finding from one-shot pruning to iterative mask search is assumed but not directly validated.

metadata.failure_mode: If the masks found via IMP/T_early are less effective after full T training than masks from IMP/T, then the ET accuracy drop could be larger than expected from the preliminary experiments. The conclusion that ET provides "≤1% drop at <95% sparsity" would be overly optimistic if the drop at intermediate sparsity for some combinations exceeds 1%.
metadata.weakness_reason: The iterative mask search in IMP includes multiple train-prune-retrain cycles, each with weight reinitialization to a rewound state. The mask discovered after several iterations may be influenced by the training dynamics over many epochs, which differ from a single training run to convergence. The preliminary experiment only evaluates the similarity of weight magnitude structure, not the convergence of iterative pruning. It is possible that iterative pruning at reduced timestep discovers masks that are less reusable than those from one-shot pruning, due to cumulative divergence.

nodes.title: ET ticket preliminary experiment uses one-shot pruning, not iterative mask search

nodes.content: For the transferability experiment, winning tickets are discovered by IMP on ANN (ReLU) and then transferred to SNN (LIF) while keeping the mask and initialization weights. Training hyperparameters used for ANN IMP (e.g., learning rate schedule, number of epochs, weight decay, batch size) are not specified. If ANN training is not optimized, the transferred tickets may be of lower quality than those from well-tuned ANN IMP, potentially biasing the comparison against SNN transfer.

metadata.failure_mode: If a properly tuned ANN IMP yields significantly better transferred tickets that maintain accuracy even at 95%+ sparsity on CIFAR10/100, then the conclusion that "ANN winning tickets transfer to SNNs only at moderate sparsity" would be false for optimal training. The claim would be an artifact of experimental setup.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper states "Transferred Ticket (i.e., initialized weight parameters and pruning mask) is discovered by IMP on ANN, and trained on SNN framework" without providing details of the ANN training protocol (e.g., architecture modifications, optimizer hyperparameters, augmentation, training epochs). It is unclear whether the ANN winning tickets are of state-of-the-art quality. Poorly trained ANN tickets may not be representative of the best possible transferred tickets, leading to an unfair comparison.

nodes.title: ANN IMP training hyperparameters for transferability experiment are unspecified

nodes.content: The transferability study is conducted on VGG16 and ResNet19 architectures. It is uncertain whether ANN→SNN transfer would succeed at higher sparsities on different architectures (e.g., deeper ResNets or architectures designed for direct spike input) where the discrepancy between ANN and SNN activations may be smaller or larger. The conclusion that transfer is limited to moderate sparsity may not generalize across the broad space of deep SNN architectures.

metadata.failure_mode: If alternative deep SNN architectures (e.g., those with fewer BN layers or different temporal processing) allow successful transfer at high sparsity, then the conclusion that "ANN winning tickets transfer to SNNs only at moderate sparsity" would be too broad, requiring qualification to the architectures tested.
metadata.weakness_reason: Only two architectures are tested. The degree of compatibility between ANN and SNN representations depends on architectural design (e.g., residual connections, BN placement, number of timesteps). Without empirical evidence across a wider range, the conclusion's scope is uncertain.

nodes.title: ANN→SNN transferability tested only on VGG16 and ResNet19

nodes.content: The SNIP failure (producing large performance degradation at high sparsity, worse than random pruning above 80% sparsity) is demonstrated on VGG16/CIFAR10. The conclusion that SNIP is ineffective for SNNs may not hold for other architectures (e.g., ResNet) or datasets (e.g., CIFAR100, SVHN), where the gradient structure at initialization may be more informative. A single experiment is insufficient to establish a general claim.

metadata.failure_mode: If SNIP works on other architectures (e.g., ResNet19 on CIFAR10) for moderate sparsity (e.g., up to 90%), then the conclusion that SNIP is "ineffective for SNNs" would be too broad, requiring scoping to VGG16-like architectures.
metadata.weakness_reason: The experiment in Fig. 9 uses only VGG16 on CIFAR10. SNIP's effectiveness depends on gradient signal-to-noise ratio at initialization, which can vary across architectures (e.g., residual connections may improve gradient flow). Without testing on other architectures or datasets, the conclusion is empirically underdetermined.

nodes.title: SNIP failure demonstrated only on VGG16/CIFAR10

nodes.content: The paper attributes SNIP's failure in SNNs to the non-differentiability of spiking neurons and the surrogate/approximated backward gradients used for training SNNs. However, the paper does not test whether using a different surrogate gradient function (e.g., with a better approximation of the true gradient) could improve SNIP's performance. The causal explanation for SNIP failure is thus speculative and not directly supported by experiments that vary the surrogate function.

metadata.failure_mode: If a different surrogate gradient function (e.g., a steeper one) at initialization yields usable SNIP masks up to 90% sparsity, the conclusion that "pruning‑at‑initialization (SNIP) is ineffective for SNNs" would be false for that surrogate. The paper's explanation would be incorrect, and the practical recommendation would be invalid.
metadata.weakness_reason: The surrogate gradient used in the paper is not specified (likely default from SpikingJelly, possibly arctan or rectangular). There exist many surrogate functions (e.g., fast-sigmoid, super-spike). If some surrogate functions provide better gradient estimates at initialization, SNIP's connection sensitivity scores could become more reliable. The paper does not explore this. Additionally, SNIP in ANNs also fails at high sparsity (Fig. 9 shows ANN SNIP degrades significantly above 80% sparsity), so the SNN failure might be quantitatively different but not qualitatively unique to SNNs. The attribution to non-differentiability is not uniquely established.

nodes.title: Causal explanation for SNIP failure is not experimentally validated by varying surrogate gradient function

nodes.content: The comparison of global pruning vs. local pruning is conducted on VGG16/CIFAR10, where global pruning yields better accuracy especially at high sparsity. The conclusion that global pruning yields better accuracy, especially at high sparsity, may not hold for residual networks (ResNet) where large variations in layer widths and skip connections alter the pruning dynamics. The paper does not provide evidence for ResNet or for other datasets.

metadata.failure_mode: If for ResNet19 global pruning is inferior or comparable to local pruning at high sparsity, then the conclusion that global pruning outperforms local pruning in deep SNNs would be false for that family of architectures. The claim would need to be restricted to VGG-style networks.
metadata.weakness_reason: The architecture of VGG16 is sequential with monotonically increasing filter sizes; ResNet has shortcut connections and different width patterns. Global pruning's tendency to sparsify deeper layers more (Fig. 6(c)) may benefit sequential architectures but could harm residual architectures where certain layers must retain specific connections to propagate gradients. Without testing on ResNet, the conclusion is architecture-specific.

nodes.title: Global vs local pruning comparison performed only on VGG16/CIFAR10

nodes.content: Spike count per image measured on CIFAR10 for VGG16 and ResNet19 shows no reduction with weight sparsity up to 98%. The conclusion that weight sparsity from LTH does not reduce spike counts may not hold for datasets with different temporal statistics (e.g., event-based datasets with higher temporal resolution) or for other pruning methods (e.g., structured pruning, EB) that produce different connectivity patterns, which could affect firing rates.

metadata.failure_mode: If on event-based datasets or with different pruning methods, weight sparsity reduces spike counts, then the conclusion that LTH weight sparsity does not reduce spike counts would be too narrow, requiring restriction to static image datasets and IMP-derived sparsity.
metadata.weakness_reason: The measurement is on static image datasets (CIFAR10) with rate coding; spike counts may be more influenced by input statistics than by weight sparsity. For event-based datasets (e.g., N-MNIST, DVS-CIFAR10), the temporal dynamics differ, and weight sparsity could have a different effect. Also, the paper uses IMP which produces specific sparsity patterns; other pruning methods might create different patterns that alter firing.

nodes.title: Spike count measured only on CIFAR10 with IMP pruning

nodes.content: The spike count is measured as total spikes per image across all layers. The paper does not analyze spike distributions per layer; it is possible that some layers have reduced spikes while others increase, leaving the total constant. The conclusion that spike energy remains similar may mask layer-specific changes that could impact hardware mapping (e.g., if deep layers become more active, they may create bottlenecks).

metadata.failure_mode: If the total spike count remains constant but spikes become concentrated in fewer layers (e.g., deep layers increase while shallow layers decrease), then energy consumption of those layers could increase, potentially causing hotspots or requiring different energy management. The conclusion that energy remains similar would be correct in aggregate but misleading for hardware implementation, which cares about distribution.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper averages spikes over all timesteps and layers. In hardware, per-layer spike rates affect local energy consumption and on-chip buffer sizes. Even if total spikes are constant, redistribution could cause certain layers to become energy bottlenecks or exceed hardware limits. The conclusion's practical implication about energy efficiency is insufficiently nuanced.

nodes.title: Aggregate spike count measurement may hide per-layer variation

nodes.content: The rewinding epoch analysis (testing accuracy at four sparsity levels across different rewinding epochs) is performed on VGG16/CIFAR10 only, where accuracy is stable up to 95.69% sparsity but shows ~1.5% drop at 98.13% sparsity when rewinding epoch is 260. The effect of rewinding epoch on IMP stability at extreme sparsity may differ for ResNet architectures or for CIFAR100, where the optimal rewinding point could be earlier or later. The paper's recommendation to use epoch 20 as default is not validated beyond this single configuration.

metadata.failure_mode: If for ResNet19/CIFAR100 the optimal rewinding epoch is different (e.g., epoch 40), practitioners following the paper's default epoch 20 might obtain suboptimal results at extreme sparsity, contradicting the conclusion that careful selection is required but no guidance beyond the tested setting is provided. The conclusion that selection affects results holds, but the practical recommendation is weak.
metadata.weakness_reason: The sensitivity of rewinding epoch is shown for one architecture and one dataset. The training dynamics vary with dataset complexity (e.g., CIFAR100 may require more epochs to stabilize) and architecture depth (ResNet has BN that affects which epoch features mature). Without broader evidence, the conclusion about "careful rewind‑epoch selection required" is supported for the tested case, but its generality is uncertain.

nodes.title: Rewinding epoch analysis performed only on VGG16/CIFAR10

nodes.content: For ResNet19 on CIFAR10, the IMP-based winning ticket at 97.54% weight sparsity achieves 93.18% test accuracy (baseline: 93.22%), a drop of only 0.04%. For the same architecture and dataset, the prior gradient-rewiring method (Chen et al., 2021) at 97.56% sparsity shows a drop of 2.10% relative to its baseline (93.22% vs 91.12%). This direct comparison on identical architecture, dataset, and similar sparsity level shows that LTH-based pruning substantially outperforms the previous state-of-the-art SNN pruning method.

metadata.credit: This highlight guards against the failure mode where LTH might be no better than existing SNN pruning methods at deep scales. It underwrites the layer of quantitative magnitude: IMP on SNNs achieves nearly lossless compression at 97.5% sparsity, while a recent competitive method exhibits significant degradation. The scope of credit is full underwriting of the claim that winning tickets exist with small degradation, at least for CIFAR10, by showing that prior methods fail where IMP succeeds.

nodes.title: IMP outperforms prior SNN pruning methods on deep architectures

nodes.content: For the VGG16 and ResNet19 SNNs trained with surrogate-gradient backpropagation on SVHN, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR10, and CIFAR100, the test accuracy of winning tickets obtained by Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) with Late Rewinding (epoch 20) and by Early-Bird (EB) detection (q=5, τ=0.02) is reported as the mean over 5 independent random seeds, with standard deviation shown as error bars at each sparsity level (0% to 98%). The small error bars indicate low inter-run variability.

metadata.credit: This guards against the failure mode where the existence claim might be a fluke of a single trial. It underwrites the layer of uncertainty quantification: the conclusion that winning tickets exist is supported by reproducible evidence across seeds. The scope of credit is quantitative tightening: the ±range indicates that inter-run variability is small, increasing confidence that the result is consistent.

nodes.title: Statistical robustness through multiple random runs

nodes.content: For four target sparsity levels (68.30%, 89.91%, 95.69%, 98.13%), the paper reports the mean GPU search time for IMP on VGG16 and ResNet19 for CIFAR10 and CIFAR100. For example, ResNet19/CIFAR10 IMP times: 21.01, 42.20, 58.91, 73.54 hours. These detailed, multi-level measurements allow practitioners to estimate search costs for their target sparsity.

metadata.credit: This guards against the failure mode where the computational expense of IMP is asserted without concrete evidence. It underwrites the layer of quantitative magnitude: the claim that IMP is expensive is supported by precise hours that increase monotonically with desired sparsity. The scope of credit is full underwriting of the cost claim.

nodes.title: Detailed multi-level search time characterization

nodes.content: On VGG16/CIFAR10 at 98.13% sparsity, EB ticket search time is 0.09 hours compared to IMP's 51.99 hours (Table 1). This two-orders-of-magnitude reduction demonstrates that early mask detection dramatically lowers search cost in SNNs.

metadata.credit: This guards against the failure mode that EB might not offer significant speedup in SNNs due to different training dynamics. It underwrites the layer of quantitative magnitude: EB reduces search time to under an hour, enabling practical deployment. The scope of credit is full underwriting of the claim that EB significantly reduces search time.

nodes.title: EB ticket search time two orders lower than IMP

nodes.content: The paper shows that on SVHN and Fashion-MNIST, EB tickets achieve winning ticket performance up to ~97% sparsity, but on CIFAR10 and CIFAR100, EB accuracy degrades substantially beyond 95% sparsity (e.g., VGG16/CIFAR10 at 95.69% sparsity: 89.55% vs baseline 92.66%; IMP at same sparsity: 92.38%). This empirical mapping provides a clear boundary for EB's applicability.

metadata.credit: This guards against the failure mode of overclaiming EB's capabilities. It underwrites the layer of generalization scope: the conclusion about EB's limitations on complex datasets is supported by systematic evidence, providing practitioners with a clear threshold (≤95%) for safe use. The scope of credit is regime-bounded support, defining when EB works and when it does not.

nodes.title: Clear empirical boundary for EB applicability

nodes.content: For VGG16 and ResNet19 on CIFAR10 and CIFAR100, training dense SNNs with T_pre = {2,3,4,5}, pruning 25% of lowest-magnitude weights, reinitializing, and retraining with T_post=5 shows that for T_pre ≥ 3 the retrain accuracy is within 1% of the unpruned baseline (e.g., VGG16/CIFAR10: T_pre=3 gives 92.3% vs baseline 92.66%). This demonstrates that weight connectivity identified from fewer timesteps can be reused without significant accuracy loss.

metadata.credit: This guards against the failure mode that training with fewer timesteps may produce fundamentally different feature representations that are not reusable. It underwrites the layer of qualitative direction: important connectivity for long-timestep inference can be identified from shorter timesteps. The scope of credit is full underwriting of the core premise of ET, across two architectures and two datasets.

nodes.title: Preliminary validation of ET core premise across architectures

nodes.content: For VGG16 and ResNet19 on CIFAR10 and CIFAR100, the normalized KL divergence between class predictions at timestep t and timestep 5 shows consistent trends across training epochs (Fig. 7(b) shows curves for multiple epochs with error bars indicating low variance). This allows T_early to be determined reliably after just 2 epochs.

metadata.credit: This guards against the failure mode where the KL divergence might fluctuate significantly across training epochs, making T_early selection unstable. It underwrites the layer of error/uncertainty quantification: the choice of T_early is robust and can be made early without waiting for convergence. The scope of credit is quantitative tightening, increasing confidence in the reliability of the ET procedure.

nodes.title: KL divergence criterion consistent across epochs and datasets

nodes.content: The paper reports accuracy and search time for IMP+ET and EB+ET across four sparsity levels for VGG16/ResNet19 on CIFAR10/100 (Table 1). Speedups range from ×1.33 to ×1.59 for IMP+ET, with accuracy drops generally ≤1% below 95% sparsity (e.g., IMP+ET on VGG16/CIFAR10 at 89.91% sparsity: 92.09% vs IMP 92.54%, drop 0.45%, speedup ×1.35). This demonstrates that ET consistently reduces search cost with modest accuracy compromise.

metadata.credit: This guards against the failure mode that ET might only work in limited settings or degrade accuracy unacceptably. It underwrites the layers of quantitative magnitude (speedup factors) and error magnitude (accuracy drop). The scope of credit is full underwriting of the practical utility of ET for the tested configurations, providing a clear trade-off characterization.

nodes.title: Systematic evaluation of ET combined with IMP and EB

nodes.content: The transferability of ANN winning tickets to SNNs is evaluated on two architectures (VGG16, ResNet19) and four datasets (SVHN, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR10, CIFAR100) across four sparsity levels (68.30%, 89.91%, 95.69%, 98.13%) (Fig. 8). This extensive mapping shows where transfer succeeds (simple datasets up to 98% sparsity) and fails (complex datasets beyond 90% sparsity).

metadata.credit: This guards against the failure mode where the transferability boundary would be unknown or suggested based on limited evidence. It underwrites the layer of generalization scope: the conclusion about limited transferability on complex datasets is supported by a broad empirical sweep. The scope of credit is regime-bounded support, providing clear conditions for expected transfer success.

nodes.title: Comprehensive transferability characterization across datasets and sparsity

nodes.content: For simple datasets (SVHN, Fashion-MNIST), transferred tickets from ANN to SNN maintain accuracy within <2% of dense SNN baseline even at 98.13% sparsity (e.g., VGG16/SVHN: transferred 94.16% vs IMP SNN 94.28% at 98.13% sparsity; from Fig. 8 approximate). This demonstrates that cross-domain transfer is highly effective in low-complexity settings, providing a useful contrast to the complex dataset failure.

metadata.credit: This guards against a blanket dismissal of ANN→SNN transfer. It underwrites the layer of qualitative direction: transfer does work well for simple datasets, and the failure on complex datasets is a graded boundary, not a universal limitation. The scope of credit is regime-bounded support, sharpening the conclusion's specificity.

nodes.title: Sharp contrast of transfer success on simple vs complex datasets

nodes.content: On VGG16/CIFAR10, ANN SNIP achieves ~88% accuracy at 80% sparsity, while SNN SNIP accuracy drops to ~45% (below random pruning) at the same sparsity (Fig. 9). This direct comparison under identical architecture and dataset isolates the effect of SNN training dynamics on SNIP's failure.

metadata.credit: This guards against the failure mode that SNIP might simply be poor for any pruning at deep networks. It underwrites the layer of qualitative direction: the failure is specifically worse in SNNs than in ANNs, supporting the conclusion that SNIP is incompatible with SNNs. The scope of credit is full underwriting of the attribution to SNN-specific factors (non-differentiability).

nodes.title: Controlled ANN vs SNN comparison isolates SNN training dynamics effect

nodes.content: For VGG16/CIFAR10 under global pruning, the paper reports layer-wise sparsity for four overall sparsity levels: 68.30%, 89.91%, 95.69%, 98.13% (Fig. 6(c)). The deeper fully-connected layers (classifier) reach >90% sparsity even at the lowest overall sparsity, while early convolutional layers stay relatively dense. This provides quantitative evidence for the claim that deeper layers become sparser under global pruning.

metadata.credit: This guards against the failure mode that the claim about deeper layers being sparser is based on intuition without data. It underwrites the layer of qualitative and quantitative magnitude: the trend is clear and monotonic across sparsity levels. The scope of credit is full underwriting for the tested VGG16 configuration.

nodes.title: Quantitative layer-wise sparsity profiles under global pruning

nodes.content: For VGG16 and ResNet19 on CIFAR10, the paper measures spikes per image across 5 sparsity levels (0%, 68.30%, 89.91%, 95.69%, 98.13%) using IMP (Fig. 10). The number of spikes remains nearly constant (e.g., VGG16: ~37k spikes at 0% sparsity, ~37k at 98.13% sparsity). Error bars from 5 runs are shown. The trend is clear and consistent across architectures.

metadata.credit: This guards against the failure mode where one might assume weight sparsity reduces spike count without measurement. It underwrites the layer of quantitative magnitude: the lack of spike reduction is empirically established across a wide sparsity range and two architectures. The scope of credit is full underwriting of the conclusion for the tested configurations.

nodes.title: Systematic spike count measurement across sparsity and architectures

nodes.content: For VGG16/CIFAR10 with IMP, the paper shows the effect of rewinding epoch (0, 5, 20, 50, 100, 300) on test accuracy at four sparsity levels: 68.30%, 89.91%, 95.69%, 98.13% (Fig. 6(a)). At ≤95.69% sparsity, accuracy is stable within ±0.5% across all rewinding epochs. At 98.13% sparsity, accuracy varies by ~1.5% (e.g., epoch 0: 91.0%, epoch 20: 91.8%, epoch 260: 90.8%). This provides quantitative guidance for rewinding epoch selection.

metadata.credit: This guards against the failure mode where the impact of rewinding epoch on deep SNNs is unknown. It underwrites the layer of quantitative magnitude and error quantification: the sensitivity is low at moderate sparsity but significant at extreme sparsity. The scope of credit is full underwriting of the claim that careful selection matters, with a concrete example of the effect size.

nodes.title: Systematic rewinding epoch sensitivity analysis

steps.reasoning: Treat as established the upstream results: accept that IMP with Late Rewinding discovers high-quality winning tickets but is computationally expensive (conclusion 2) and that EB reduces search time but cannot reach the very highest sparsities on complex datasets (conclusion 3); these upstream results are used as background to frame the empirical demonstration of the existence of winning tickets in deep SNNs up to ≈97% sparsity. [21]

Define "winning ticket" per the authors' operationalization: given a dense network $f(x;\theta)$ with parameters $\theta\in\mathbb{R}^n$, a pruning mask $m\in\{0,1\}^n$ defines the subnetwork $f(x;\theta\odot m)$ where $\odot$ denotes elementwise multiplication; in the IMP procedure the authors iteratively prune the $p\%$ lowest-absolute-value weights per IMP iteration and reinitialize to rewound weights (Late Rewinding epoch = 20), and they call the resulting pruned-and-rewound subnetwork a "winning ticket" when it achieves comparable test accuracy to the unpruned dense SNN. [21]

State the core experimental claim: the authors conduct extensive experiments on two deep SNN architectures (VGG16 and ResNet19) across four datasets (SVHN, Fashion‑MNIST, CIFAR10 and CIFAR100) using surrogate-gradient backpropagation for SNN training, and by applying IMP with Late Rewinding (rewind-to-epoch-20) they observe that winning tickets exist in these deep SNNs at very high sparsity levels—up to approximately 97% sparsity—while preserving test accuracy comparable to the dense baseline (small degradations). The authors present accuracy-vs-sparsity plots and tabulated comparisons to support this. Fig. 5

Give the concrete exemplar numeric result: in the ResNet19/CIFAR10 configuration the dense baseline accuracy is reported as 93.22%; under the authors' IMP procedure with Late Rewinding they report a pruned model at 97.54% sparsity with accuracy degraded by only −0.04% relative to the baseline (i.e., essentially preserving baseline accuracy), a numerical example explicitly shown in their comparison table. Table 2

Summarize the method-of-construction for a winning ticket as used in experiments: the winning ticket reported is the subnetwork $f(x;\theta\odot m)$ obtained by iterative pruning of the $p\%$ lowest-magnitude weights per IMP iteration (the per-iteration pruning fraction used in experiments is $p=25\%$ in the described IMP protocol with $K$ iterations) and reinitializing to the rewound weights at epoch 20 (Late Rewinding), with IMP applied using global magnitude pruning across layers. [21]

Conclude the existence claim: therefore, a dense deep SNN trained with surrogate-gradient backpropagation contains sparse subnetworks ("winning tickets") that achieve comparable test accuracy to the unpruned dense SNN: using Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) with Late Rewinding (rewind to epoch 20), experiments on VGG16 and ResNet19 SNNs across datasets SVHN, Fashion‑MNIST, CIFAR10 and CIFAR100 demonstrate winning tickets at up to ~97% sparsity with small accuracy degradation (for example, on ResNet19/CIFAR10 the baseline accuracy 93.22% is preserved within −0.04% at 97.54% sparsity reported under IMP). Fig. 5

State the starting points used for this derivation: accept as established the upstream conclusions that Late Rewinding stabilizes IMP for deep SNNs (conclusion 9) and that global magnitude pruning yields better accuracy than per-layer local pruning and produces particular layer-wise sparsity profiles (conclusion 7); treat these as known facts in reconstructing why IMP finds high-quality winning tickets but is computationally expensive on SNNs. [22]

Explain how IMP is configured and evaluated in the experiments: define IMP (Iterative Magnitude Pruning) as the procedure that repeatedly trains the network to convergence, removes the $p\%$ lowest-magnitude weights to create mask $m_k$, reinitializes (here with Late Rewinding to epoch 20), and repeats for $K$ iterations until the target sparsity is reached; in the authors' runs they set per-iteration pruning $p=25\%$ and $K=15$ iterations in some protocols, and they apply global magnitude pruning (per conclusion 7) along with Late Rewinding (per conclusion 9) to obtain stable, high-performing sparse SNNs. [21]

Present the empirical accuracy result showing IMP finds high-quality winning tickets: the authors report that IMP (with Late Rewinding and global pruning) discovers winning tickets reaching up to ≈97% sparsity while preserving test accuracy close to or matching the dense baseline across multiple architectures and datasets; for example, in their ResNet19/CIFAR10 experiments the dense baseline accuracy is 93.22% and IMP yields a pruned network at 97.54% sparsity with an accuracy drop of only −0.04% (i.e., preserving baseline accuracy within −0.04%). These accuracy results are summarized in the comparative results table. Table 2

Document the computational cost of IMP on SNNs: the authors explicitly measure and report "winning-ticket search time" (GPU-hours) for IMP across multiple configurations in their timing table (Table 1). The reported IMP search times for larger sparsity targets are substantial—ranging from tens of GPU-hours up to approximately 73.54 GPU-hours for ResNet19 on CIFAR10 at 98.13% target sparsity (listed IMP times for ResNet19/CIFAR10 are 21.01, 42.20, 58.91, 73.54 hours corresponding to increasing sparsity levels in the table). The authors summarize that searching for sparsity ≥95% requires on the order of dozens of GPU-hours per configuration. Table 1

Relate the computational cost to SNN-specific factors: the authors note that IMP's iterative training–pruning–retraining loop is especially costly in SNNs because each training epoch itself is more expensive due to multiple feedforward timesteps (default $T=5$ in their experiments); they therefore motivate temporal-cost-reduction techniques (the Early-Time ticket) and early-mask detection (EB) because IMP's runtimes become large when combined with SNN timestep multiplicity. The paper's discussion and timing measurements make this connection explicit. Table 1

Conclude the combined statement: thus, Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) with Late Rewinding and global pruning discovers high‑quality winning tickets in deep SNNs (achieving top accuracies across sparsity levels), but the iterative search is computationally costly for SNNs—measured GPU search times in the authors' experiments range from tens to ~73.54 hours for extreme sparsity (ResNet19/CIFAR10 at 98.13% took 73.54 hours), and searching for ≥95% sparsity requires dozens of GPU-hours per configuration. Table 1

Define EB = Early-Bird ticket detection as the procedure that, at a searching iteration $k$, obtains a pruning mask $m_k$ and measures the mask difference between $m_k$ and the previous $q$ masks $m_{k-1},m_{k-2},\dots,m_{k-q}$; if the maximum difference is less than a threshold $\tau$, the algorithm stops and returns $m_k$ as the EB ticket. In the experiments the authors set the time window $q=5$ and threshold $\tau=0.02$, and they replaced the original channel-pruning EB with unstructured weight pruning to match other pruning methods' sparsity levels. [80]

Describe the experimental observation that EB discovers stable pruning masks early in training for SNNs: the authors measure the epoch at which EB's mask-difference criterion is met and report that EB often finishes discovering a mask within a small number of training hours on GPU (per-configuration EB search times in the authors' experiments are substantially smaller than IMP's search times). Evidence for the low EB search times appears in the tabulated search-time results (Table 1) where EB search times across configurations are on the order of minutes to a few hours (for example, EB search times shown for VGG16/CIFAR10 are 1.96, 0.74, 0.11, 0.09 hours for different sparsities). Table 1

From the data in Table 1, quantify the EB search-time reductions: define "search time" as the GPU-hours the authors report for discovering the pruning mask; across multiple architectures and datasets EB search times are typically below 2 hours (for VGG16/CIFAR10 the largest reported EB entry is 1.96 hours; for ResNet19/CIFAR10 EB entries are 2.49, 0.87, 0.24, 0.08 hours), supporting the claim that EB "dramatically reduces" search time compared to iterative methods. Table 1

Report the EB success versus dataset complexity: the authors compare winning-ticket accuracy-versus-sparsity curves (their Figure showing accuracy with respect to sparsity and the performance comparison across pruning methods) and explicitly state that EB finds winning tickets exceeding 95% sparsity for relatively simple datasets (SVHN and Fashion-MNIST) but fails to find winning tickets beyond ≈95% sparsity for the more complex datasets CIFAR10 and CIFAR100, where accuracy degrades substantially above that sparsity. This observation is summarized in the text accompanying the accuracy plots and in the figure that compares pruning methods (the accuracy-vs-sparsity plot and related discussion). Fig. 5

State the combined empirical conclusion: EB (Early-Bird) tickets, implemented with unstructured pruning and hyperparameters $q=5$, $\tau=0.02$, discover stable masks early and therefore cut winning-ticket search time dramatically (search often completes within ≲2 GPU-hours in the authors' reported configurations). However, EB does not reliably reach the very highest sparsity levels on complex image datasets: EB reliably finds winning tickets up to approximately 95% sparsity on simple datasets (SVHN, Fashion-MNIST) but cannot reach winning tickets >95% sparsity on CIFAR10 and CIFAR100, where accuracy drops substantially beyond that sparsity threshold. Fig. 7(a)

Start from the established upstream results: accept that IMP finds high-quality winning tickets though at high computational cost (conclusion 2) and that EB discovers masks early reducing search time but has sparsity limitations (conclusion 3); these motivate a temporal search-cost reduction technique that leverages SNNs' multi-timestep processing. Table 1

Define the temporal quantities and the representation used: let $T$ denote the original number of timesteps used to run the SNN when training to the target performance, and for any $t\in\{1,\dots,T\}$ let $P_t$ denote the class-probability vector obtained by accumulating the output-layer activations from timestep $1$ through $t$ (i.e., accumulated outputs across timesteps produce $P_t$). The authors set the default timestep $T=5$ in experiments. Define $T_{early}$ as a smaller timestep to be selected for searching connectivity. Algorithm 1

Introduce and reproduce the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence criterion used to choose $T_{early}$: the KL divergence between $P_{t}$ and $P_{T}$ is computed as
$D_{KL}(P_{t}\|P_{T})=\sum_x P_{t}(x)\ln\frac{P_{t}(x)}{P_{T}(x)}$.
The authors normalize these values by dividing by $D_{KL}(P_2\|P_T)$ to obtain normalized divergences $\hat{D}_{KL}(P_t\|P_T)=\frac{D_{KL}(P_t\|P_T)}{D_{KL}(P_2\|P_T)}$, and they select the smallest $t$ such that $\hat{D}_{KL}(P_t\|P_T)<\lambda$ where $\lambda$ is a threshold hyperparameter (the authors use $\lambda=0.6$ in most experiments). This selection procedure is given explicitly as the core of the Early‑Time selection algorithm. Fig. 4

Describe the algorithmic application of ET to winning-ticket search: denote $F(\cdot)$ as the winning-ticket search procedure (either IMP or EB). The ET procedure first runs a small number of initial training epochs ($N=2$ in experiments) for stability, then computes accumulated class probabilities $P_t$ for $t=2,\dots,T$, computes and normalizes KL divergences, selects $T_{early}$ as the minimal $t$ with normalized KL divergence below $\lambda$, runs the chosen search method $F$ using the smaller timestep $T_{early}$ to discover the pruning mask (i.e., WinningTicket ← $F$(SNN,$T_{early}$)), and finally trains the discovered (pruned) network with the original full timestep $T$ to obtain the final pruned SNN. This procedure is reproduced in the paper's algorithm (Algorithm 1). Algorithm 1

Present empirical results quantifying ET's benefits and costs: the authors apply ET combined with either IMP or EB and report measured search-time speedups and accuracy changes in Table 1; across the reported configurations ET reduces winning-ticket search time substantially (reported speedup factors up to approximately $\times1.66$ in the paper's summary; the per-configuration table shows many speedups in the $\times1.3$–$\times1.6$ range), while incurring relatively small accuracy degradations in many cases (for sparsities less than 95% the drop is typically ≤~1% in several experiments). Specific numbers include, for ResNet19/CIFAR10 using IMP, original IMP search time 73.54 hours at 98.13% sparsity versus IMP+ET search time 46.40 hours (speedup ≈$\times$1.58) with an accuracy change reported in the table. These empirical data support the claim that ET reduces search time substantially while incurring only small accuracy reductions for moderate sparsity targets. Table 1

Report stability of ET selection: the authors observe that normalized KL-divergence curves are fairly consistent across training epochs, enabling $T_{early}$ to be determined stably after a small number $N$ of initial epochs; they explicitly use $N=2$ epochs in experiments for stability and demonstrate in the experiments that $T_{early}$ chosen this way leads to the reported speedups and small accuracy impacts. The paper also shows a hyperparameter sweep of $\lambda$ vs selected $T_{early}$ and the resulting accuracies to demonstrate practical behavior. Fig. 7(b)

Conclude the defined ET ticket properties: Early‑Time (ET) ticket is therefore a temporal search‑cost reduction technique that finds important weight connectivity for an SNN trained for $T$ timesteps by first training with a smaller timestep $T_{early}<T$ selected via the normalized KL‑divergence criterion $D_{KL}(P_t\|P_T)/D_{KL}(P_2\|P_T)<\lambda$; ET is applied to the winning‑ticket search procedure $F(\cdot)$ (IMP or EB) by discovering the mask with $T_{early}$ and then training the pruned network at the original $T$, and empirically ET combined with IMP or EB reduces winning‑ticket search time substantially (measured speedups up to ~$\times1.66$ in reported configurations) while incurring small accuracy reductions (≤~1% drop for sparsity <95% in many experiments). Fig. 3

Define the transfer experiment: "Transferred Ticket" means the initialization weights and pruning mask discovered by Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) applied to an Artificial Neural Network (ANN) with ReLU activations; the transferred configuration is then used to initialize and train a Spiking Neural Network (SNN) where the ReLU activations are replaced by Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) spiking neurons and training proceeds under the SNN framework. The authors implement this by discovering IMP masks on ANNs and then training the same mask+initialization in the SNN setting. [21]

Report empirical outcomes for simple datasets: in the authors' cross-architecture, cross-dataset experiments (illustrated in the transferability figure), for relatively simple datasets SVHN and Fashion-MNIST the transferred ANN→SNN tickets exhibit small accuracy degradation even at extreme sparsity in some runs; the authors state these transfers show less than approximately 2% accuracy drop for those simple datasets at high sparsity levels (e.g., up to 98.13% sparsity in reported runs). The claim is reported in the transferability section discussion and visualized in the transferability plot. Fig. 8

Report empirical outcomes for complex datasets: for more complex datasets (CIFAR10 and CIFAR100) the authors report that the Transferred Ticket fails to preserve accuracy at high sparsity; specifically, transferred tickets exhibit large accuracy degradation at high sparsity (≥95%), with substantial performance loss visible in the transferability plots and stated explicitly in the text accompanying those plots.
