The authors conclude that ANN-found winning tickets and SNN-winning tickets only partially overlap, and that ANN-based searching cannot fully substitute SNN search for high-sparsity targets. Fig. 8

Quantify the computational advantage of ANN search: the authors report that discovering the winning ticket from an ANN for 98.13% sparsity requires approximately 14 GPU-hours, which they note is roughly 5× faster than the IMP search on SNNs for the same sparsity in their experiments; this supports the claim that ANN-to-SNN transfer can reduce search cost, albeit with limited transferability at high sparsity. Fig. 8

Synthesize the conclusion: therefore, winning tickets discovered by IMP on ANNs can transfer to SNNs with modest success at low-to-moderate sparsity—transfer works well on simple datasets (SVHN, Fashion-MNIST) with small (<~2%) accuracy drops even at extreme sparsity in some runs—but for complex datasets (CIFAR10, CIFAR100) transferred tickets suffer large accuracy degradation at high sparsity (≥95%), demonstrating only partial commonality between ANN and SNN winning tickets. Fig. 8

Define SNIP: SNIP is a pruning-at-initialization algorithm that computes an importance score for each weight from the magnitude of initial backward gradients (i.e., connection sensitivity at initialization) and prunes a single-shot set of weights prior to training; the authors evaluate SNIP in the SNN context and explicitly identify SNIP as the representative pruning-at-initialization method considered. [41]

Present the experimental observation: in the authors' VGG16/CIFAR10 experiments the SNN pruned by SNIP suffers severe accuracy degradation at high sparsity ($>80\%$) and in some cases performs worse than random pruning; this empirical behavior is shown in the performance-comparison figure for SNIP on ANN vs SNIP on SNN. The authors state that SNNs show "huge performance degradation at high sparsity regime ($>80\%$), even worse than random pruning." Fig. 9

Explain the attributed cause from the authors' text: the authors attribute SNIP's failure in SNNs to the non-differentiable input–output transfer function of the LIF spiking neuron and to the use of surrogate/approximated backward gradients during SNN training; because SNIP's importance estimates rely on accurate initial backward gradients, the surrogate/approximated gradients in SNNs undermine the reliability of SNIP's sensitivity scores at initialization. This attribution is stated explicitly in the paper. [54]

Conclude that SNIP is ineffective for deep SNNs: combining the experimental degradation at high sparsity and the authors' stated attribution leads to the conclusion that SNIP fails to produce working winning tickets for deep SNNs—SNIP produces large performance degradation at high sparsity (>80%) and can be worse than random pruning in the reported experiments. Fig. 9

Define global magnitude pruning and local (per-layer) pruning: global magnitude pruning selects the lowest-magnitude weights across the entire network to meet a global sparsity target, whereas local pruning applies the same pruning percentage independently within each layer. The authors implement global pruning when running IMP experiments and explicitly compare it to layer-local pruning. [21]

Present the empirical comparison: the authors compare global pruning and local pruning on VGG16/CIFAR10 and report that global pruning achieves better accuracy than local pruning, especially at high target sparsity levels; this comparison is presented in the plotted results and the accompanying text which states "global pruning achieves better performance than local pruning, especially for high sparsity levels." Fig. 6(b)

Report layer-wise sparsity profile under global pruning: the authors plot the per-layer sparsity resulting from global pruning on VGG16/CIFAR10 and observe that deeper layers tend to be pruned to higher sparsity (i.e., deep layers end up with fewer retained weights) compared to shallower layers under the global-magnitude criterion; this observation is shown in the layer-wise sparsity visualization. Fig. 6(c)

Synthesize the conclusion: therefore, global magnitude pruning yields better accuracy in deep SNNs than applying identical per-layer local pruning percentages, and under global pruning the layer-wise sparsity profile shows deeper layers become sparser (shallow layers retain relatively more weights); in the authors' VGG16/CIFAR10 experiments this global strategy produces superior performance particularly at high sparsity targets. Fig. 6(b)

Define spike count and its relevance: the "number of spikes per image" is the total count of spiking events generated by the network when processing one input image across all neurons and all timesteps; the authors note that spike count largely determines SNN multiply–accumulate (MAC) compute energy. Introduce the claim under test: whether weight sparsity obtained from Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) pruning reduces spike rates (and thus spike-driven compute energy). [1]

Describe the measurement protocol: the authors prune networks using IMP, then measure the number of spikes per image across a range of weight sparsities for VGG16 and ResNet19 on CIFAR10; the plotted results show the spike counts as a function of weight sparsity. Fig. 10

Report the empirical outcome: the plotted measurements (Fig. 10) demonstrate that the number of spikes per image remains approximately constant across a wide range of weight sparsities for both VGG16 and ResNet19 on CIFAR10 when pruning is performed by IMP, i.e., sparse SNNs obtained via LTH maintain similar spike rates compared to dense networks. Fig. 10

Interpret energy implications as stated by the authors: because spike counts (and thus spike-driven MAC activity) do not decrease with weight sparsity in these experiments, weight sparsity from LTH primarily reduces the memory footprint and the energy costs related to memory movement rather than lowering spike‑driven compute energy; the authors reference prior work that with over 98% sparse weights memory-movement energy can be reduced substantially (up to a quoted factor), but they emphasize that spike energy remains similar empirically. [6]

Define Late Rewinding: Late Rewinding is the modification to the Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) procedure in which, after pruning to obtain mask $m_k$, the network is reinitialized not to the original random initialization but to the network weights at some intermediate training epoch $i$ (i.e., "rewind to epoch $i$") before retraining and repeating the pruning iterations. The authors state they apply Late Rewinding and specifically use rewind epoch $i=20$ in their experiments on SNNs. [22]

Present the empirical advantage of Late Rewinding: the authors report that Late Rewinding provides more stable starting points for subsequent retraining-pruning iterations in IMP and that, when applied to deep SNNs, Late Rewinding shows better performance at high sparsity than rewinding to the original initialization; this qualitative claim is supported by experimental comparisons referenced in the paper (the authors state "we found that Late Rewinding shows better performance than the original IMP in deep SNNs"). Table 2

Show sensitivity to rewind-epoch selection at extreme sparsity: the authors vary the rewinding epoch and plot resulting accuracies across sparsity levels (their plotted results for rewinding epoch vs. accuracy). The experiments show that for sparsities up to 95.69% the rewinding epoch does not cause a large accuracy change, but at very high sparsity (98.13%) the rewinding epoch can substantially affect accuracy—for example, the authors report a non-trivial accuracy drop around 1.5% at rewinding epoch 260 for the extreme sparsity case—indicating that the choice of rewind epoch matters in extreme-sparsity regimes. Fig. 6(a)

Conclude the role of Late Rewinding in stabilizing IMP for SNNs: therefore, using Late Rewinding (rewinding to intermediate training epochs such as epoch 20 used by the authors) improves IMP's stability and empirical performance for deep SNNs at high sparsity compared to rewinding to initialization, but careful selection of the rewinding epoch is required because the rewind epoch can noticeably affect accuracy in extreme-sparsity settings. Fig. 6(a)

open_questions.content: The paper identifies several unresolved scientific and practical issues for future work: (1) an accuracy–computational‑cost tradeoff when applying ET: ET reduces search time but the ET‑derived winning tickets do not perfectly match full‑T IMP tickets (the authors observe small but nonzero accuracy gaps, particularly at extreme sparsity), so quantifying and controlling this tradeoff across architectures and datasets remains open; (2) sensitivity to hyperparameters and heuristics: selection of KL threshold λ for ET and the rewinding epoch for IMP materially affect performance in high‑sparsity regimes, and the paper reports empirical defaults (λ=0.6, rewind epoch=20) but leaves systematic optimization and theoretical justification of these choices unresolved; (3) limited transferability from ANN to SNN at high sparsity: while ANN→SNN transfer reduces search cost for simple datasets, transferred tickets fail at ≥95% sparsity on complex datasets (CIFAR10/CIFAR100); understanding the structural causes of this breakdown and whether adapted transfer schemes can close the gap is unresolved; (4) incompatibility of gradient‑based pruning‑at‑initialization (e.g., SNIP) with surrogate/approximated gradients in SNNs: SNIP failed in experiments, and designing initialization‑time scoring methods that account for spiking non‑differentiability is an open challenge; (5) energy implications beyond weight sparsity: LTH weight sparsity does not reduce spike counts in the measured setups, so achieving joint reductions of memory movement and spike MAC energy (e.g., via co‑design of pruning and temporal/spike‑rate mechanisms) is an open engineering and scientific problem.
